questions.q: Which otoscopic finding does the module identify as the single most reliable sign of acute otitis media?
ch: Tenderness on traction of the auricle with a swollen external canal
A retracted tympanic membrane with normal mobility on insufflation
Loss of the light reflex as the only abnormality on the membrane
An erythematous tympanic membrane alone in a crying, febrile toddler
Moderate-to-severe bulging of the tympanic membrane
questions.exp: A bulging tympanic membrane is the single most reliable sign of AOM, and the AAP criteria require moderate-to-severe bulging (or new otorrhea) to make the diagnosis.
why: Canal swelling with pain on auricular traction describes otitis externa, which the criteria specifically exclude.
A retracted, normally mobile membrane argues against an acutely infected middle-ear effusion.
Loss of the light reflex accompanies the bulging membrane but is not the most reliable single sign.
A red membrane alone can be produced by crying or fever and does not qualify as AOM.

questions.q: Which trio of organisms does the module list as the top bacterial pathogens in acute otitis media?
ch: Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Proteus mirabilis
Neisseria meningitidis, Listeria monocytogenes, and group B Streptococcus
Streptococcus pneumoniae, nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis
Group A Streptococcus, Escherichia coli, and Klebsiella pneumoniae
Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, and Legionella species
questions.exp: The classic middle-ear trio is Streptococcus pneumoniae, nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis, although many episodes of AOM are viral or self-limited.
why: Pseudomonas and Proteus belong to canal and chronic-drainage disease rather than acute otitis media.
These are neonatal meningitis and sepsis organisms, not the middle-ear trio.
Group A Streptococcus and enteric gram-negatives are not the pathogens the module highlights.
These atypical respiratory organisms are not among the middle-ear pathogens the module names.

questions.q: Why does the module say acute otitis media peaks in children 6 to 24 months old?
ch: The mastoid air cells are fully pneumatized and seed the middle-ear cleft directly
Their Eustachian tubes are shorter, more horizontal, and floppier than an adult's
Their tympanic membranes are thicker and rupture far less readily than an adult's
They have not yet developed any mucosal immunity to respiratory viruses at all
Middle-ear pressure is normally positive at this age and traps infected secretions
questions.exp: The 6-24 month peak is attributed to Eustachian tube anatomy: shorter, more horizontal, and more floppy tubes than an adult's, which impairs middle-ear ventilation after a viral URI.
why: Mastoid pneumatization is discussed as a complication site (mastoiditis), not as the cause.
Membrane thickness is not the mechanism the module gives for the age distribution.
The module ties the peak to tube anatomy, not to a complete absence of viral immunity.
The module describes negative middle-ear pressure with effusion, not positive pressure.

questions.q: Pneumatic otoscopy is described as the confirmatory exam in acute otitis media. Which result supports the diagnosis?
ch: A normal-appearing membrane whose mobility is preserved once the child stops crying
A retracted membrane with exaggerated excursion on insufflation of the ear canal
A bulging, opaque membrane with reduced or absent mobility and loss of the light reflex
A translucent membrane that moves briskly with both positive and negative pressure
A mobile membrane with a crisp light reflex and clearly visible ossicular landmarks
questions.exp: The confirmatory exam is pneumatic otoscopy showing a bulging, opaque tympanic membrane with reduced or absent mobility and loss of the light reflex; tympanometry is the backup when otoscopy is equivocal.
why: A normal membrane with preserved mobility does not meet the diagnostic criteria for AOM.
Retraction with exaggerated excursion is not the pattern the module attributes to AOM.
Brisk movement of a translucent membrane is a normal exam and excludes an acute effusion.
Preserved mobility with a crisp light reflex describes a normal middle ear.

questions.q: A 2-year-old with no drug allergies is started on high-dose amoxicillin, roughly 80-90 mg/kg/day divided twice daily, for acute otitis media. Why is the dose high?
ch: To raise middle-ear drug levels above the MIC of penicillin-intermediate S. pneumoniae
To allow the whole treatment course to be compressed into a single observed dose
To achieve therapeutic concentrations in cerebrospinal fluid should meningitis follow
To provide reliable coverage for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus
To overcome beta-lactamase produced by Moraxella catarrhalis and H. influenzae
questions.exp: High-dose amoxicillin raises middle-ear fluid concentrations above the MIC of penicillin-intermediate pneumococci, whose resistance comes from altered penicillin-binding proteins rather than beta-lactamase.
why: The module keeps a full course with reassessment at 48-72 hours, not a single dose.
Dosing is aimed at middle-ear fluid levels; CSF penetration is not the stated rationale.
MRSA is not among the middle-ear pathogens this module treats with amoxicillin.
Beta-lactamase producers are the reason to ADD clavulanate; a higher amoxicillin dose does not defeat that enzyme.

questions.q: A 3-year-old with acute otitis media also has purulent conjunctivitis. Which plan does the module recommend?
ch: Topical antibiotic ear drops, since the infection is confined to the external ear canal
Oral cefdinir, since conjunctivitis is treated as evidence of true penicillin allergy
High-dose amoxicillin, since concurrent conjunctivitis does not alter the likely pathogen
Amoxicillin-clavulanate, since this syndrome suggests beta-lactamase-producing H. influenzae
Observation for 48-72 hours, since conjunctivitis makes a purely viral course likely
questions.exp: AOM with purulent conjunctivitis is enriched for nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae, so the module moves to amoxicillin-clavulanate for the added beta-lactamase coverage.
why: The infection sits in the middle ear behind an intact membrane, where drops do not reach.
Cefdinir is reserved for non-severe penicillin allergy or treatment failure, not for conjunctivitis.
Concurrent purulent conjunctivitis is one of the module's explicit reasons to move off plain amoxicillin.
The module lists this syndrome as a first-line antibiotic indication, not an observation candidate.

questions.q: For which child does the module say watchful waiting is a preferred initial strategy?
ch: A child 6 months or older with unilateral non-severe AOM and reliable follow-up
Any child under 6 months of age whose fever has already broken with ibuprofen
A child with bilateral AOM, a temperature of 39.5C, and severe otalgia at rest
A child with new otorrhea draining through a perforated tympanic membrane
A child who completed a course of amoxicillin for AOM three weeks earlier
questions.exp: Observation is offered for children 6 months and older with unilateral non-severe AOM (or 24 months and older with bilateral non-severe disease) when follow-up is reliable, with antibiotics started if there is no improvement in 48-72 hours.
why: Infants under 6 months are not offered observation in the module's scheme.
Fever at or above 39C with severe otalgia defines severe disease and calls for antibiotics.
New otorrhea is itself a diagnostic criterion for AOM and prompts treatment.
Amoxicillin within the past 30 days pushes the choice toward amoxicillin-clavulanate.

questions.q: A 4-year-old has a middle-ear effusion on tympanometry but no ear pain, no fever, and no membrane bulging. How does the module direct management?
ch: Start high-dose amoxicillin, because any middle-ear effusion represents infection
This is otitis media with effusion: no antibiotics, only follow-up and hearing surveillance
Obtain CT of the temporal bones to exclude occult intracranial extension of infection
Give a single dose of IM ceftriaxone to clear the effusion before school entry
Refer for immediate tympanocentesis to identify the organism in the middle ear
questions.exp: Fluid without acute inflammation is otitis media with effusion, which should not be treated with antibiotics; it needs follow-up and hearing surveillance because persistent effusion can affect speech and school.
why: OME is effusion without acute infection, so antibiotics are explicitly not warranted.
Imaging is reserved for suspected complications such as mastoiditis or intracranial spread.
Ceftriaxone is for vomiting children or amoxicillin failure in true AOM, not for OME.
Tympanocentesis is a last resort after failed appropriate therapy, not a step in OME.

questions.q: Which element does the module insist belongs in every acute otitis media plan, whether or not an antibiotic is prescribed?
ch: A prescription for oral antihistamines to help drain the middle-ear effusion
An audiogram obtained on the same day the diagnosis is first established
A course of oral corticosteroids to shrink Eustachian tube mucosal edema
An analgesia plan with ibuprofen or acetaminophen for otalgia and fever
A repeat pneumatic otoscopy examination within the next twenty-four hours
questions.exp: Analgesia with ibuprofen or acetaminophen is a core part of every AOM plan and is emphasized regardless of whether antibiotics are given; no child should go home without a pain plan.
why: Antihistamines are not part of the module's treatment plan for AOM.
Audiology follow-up is arranged for persistent effusion or hearing concerns, not routinely at diagnosis.
Corticosteroids are not among the treatments this module lists.
Reassessment is set at 48-72 hours, not within a single day.

questions.q: A 15-month-old on day 3 of amoxicillin for acute otitis media returns with high fever, redness and swelling behind the ear, and a protruding auricle. What does this represent?
ch: Expected postauricular lymphadenopathy from the viral upper respiratory infection
A healing tympanic membrane perforation causing referred pain behind the ear
Uncomplicated treatment failure, managed with a longer oral course at home
Otitis externa from swimming, treated with topical drops and canal precautions
Acute mastoiditis, requiring urgent imaging and intravenous antibiotics
questions.exp: Postauricular erythema and swelling with a protruding auricle is the red flag for acute mastoiditis, which needs urgent imaging and IV antibiotics rather than continued oral therapy.
why: The module names this exact picture as mastoiditis, a complication, not benign adenopathy.
A perforation classically brings sudden pain relief with otorrhea, not postauricular swelling.
Treatment failure by itself does not produce postauricular swelling and a protruding ear.
Otitis externa causes canal pain and swelling, not swelling behind the auricle.

questions.q: Which description matches the anatomy of intussusception as the module defines it?
ch: Outpouching of a persistent vitelline duct remnant on the border of the ileum
Muscular hypertrophy of a bowel sphincter producing a functional outlet obstruction
A congenital narrowing of the ileocecal valve that obstructs stool passage
Twisting of the midgut around its mesenteric axis, cutting off arterial inflow
A proximal bowel segment invaginating into the distal segment, dragging its mesentery inward
questions.exp: The intussusceptum telescopes into the intussuscipiens and drags its mesentery inward, producing venous congestion, bowel-wall edema, and eventual ischemia; the classic site is ileocolic at the ileocecal valve.
why: That describes a Meckel diverticulum, which the module lists only as a possible lead point.
Sphincter muscle hypertrophy describes pyloric stenosis, not telescoping bowel.
The module describes an acquired invagination, not a congenital valve stenosis.
Twisting about the mesenteric axis is volvulus, a different mechanism entirely.

questions.q: Which test does the module call the diagnostic test of choice for suspected intussusception?
ch: Diagnostic laparoscopy performed before any attempt at enema reduction
Abdominal ultrasound, showing the target sign and the pseudokidney sign
Plain abdominal radiography, which is diagnostic when gas is absent from the RLQ
CT of the abdomen with intravenous and oral contrast in every suspected case
Stool guaiac testing, which confirms the diagnosis once it turns positive
questions.exp: Abdominal ultrasound is the diagnostic test of choice, highly sensitive and specific, with the target/donut sign on transverse view and the pseudokidney sign on longitudinal view.
why: Surgery is reserved for failed enema, perforation, peritonitis, shock, or a lead point.
Plain films are nonspecific here; they mainly help exclude free air before an enema.
CT is not the module's first-line study for this diagnosis in children.
Guaiac may be positive before gross blood appears, but it is supportive, not diagnostic.

questions.q: What is the peak age range the module gives for intussusception?
ch: 10 to 14 years, coinciding with the adolescent growth spurt
The first 3 to 6 weeks of life, as feeding volumes are increasing
School age, 5 to 10 years, following adenoviral gastroenteritis
6 months to 3 years, where disease is typically idiopathic and ileocolic
Birth to 2 weeks, as meconium clears through the terminal ileum
questions.exp: Intussusception is the most common cause of intestinal obstruction in children 6 months to 3 years, and in that window the module says to think idiopathic and ileocolic.
why: Adolescence falls outside the described window and would raise concern for a lead point.
Three to six weeks of age is the classic window for pyloric stenosis instead.
Presentation after age 2 shifts suspicion toward a pathologic lead point.
The neonatal period is not the peak the module describes.

questions.q: A parent asks whether their toddler could have intussusception without bloody stool. What does the module teach about the classic triad?
ch: The full triad of colicky pain, vomiting, and currant jelly stool appears in fewer than 25% of cases
The triad is present in nearly every case, so its absence effectively rules the diagnosis out
Bloody stool is the earliest of the three findings and precedes the onset of colicky pain
The triad applies only to children over 2 years of age who have a pathologic lead point
Vomiting is the only element of the triad that appears before bowel ischemia has begun
questions.exp: The classic triad of intermittent colicky pain, vomiting, and currant jelly stool is complete in fewer than one in four children, so its absence does not rule out intussusception; episodic lethargy alone can be the sole presentation.
why: The module says the opposite: the full triad is the exception rather than the rule.
Currant jelly stool is a late finding reflecting mucosal ischemia, not the earliest sign.
The triad is described for the typical idiopathic case, not restricted to lead-point disease.
The module does not single vomiting out this way; pain and lethargy commonly come first.

questions.q: A toddler with intermittent colicky pain passes stool mixed with blood and mucus. How should this finding be interpreted?
ch: Evidence of a coexisting bacterial enteritis rather than intussusception
A benign consequence of the contrast enema already given for reduction
A late, ominous sign of ischemic mucosa that must be reported immediately
Proof that the intussusception has already reduced itself spontaneously
An early screening finding that appears before any mucosal compromise
questions.exp: Currant jelly stool is blood plus mucus from ischemic mucosa, a late and ominous finding rather than an early screening sign; nursing guidance is to document and report its first appearance immediately.
why: The finding is attributed to ischemic bowel mucosa in this module, not to enteritis.
The stool change reflects mucosal ischemia and is not an artifact of contrast.
Bloody mucoid stool signals advancing ischemia, not spontaneous resolution.
The module explicitly warns that currant jelly stool is late, not an early screening finding.

questions.q: Which set of findings does the module list as contraindications to enema reduction?
ch: Leukocytosis, dehydration, and a first episode of colicky abdominal pain
Currant jelly stool, vomiting, and a palpable right upper quadrant mass
Age under 2 years, recent viral illness, and hypertrophied Peyer patches
Perforation, peritonitis, and hemodynamic instability
A positive ultrasound target sign with an empty right lower quadrant
questions.exp: The contraindications to enema are stated plainly as perforation, peritonitis, and shock; the child is resuscitated and surgery is involved before any reduction attempt.
why: Dehydration and leukocytosis prompt resuscitation and raise concern for ischemia, but are not the listed contraindications.
These are presenting features of intussusception itself, not reasons to withhold the enema.
Young age with a preceding viral illness describes the typical idiopathic case that gets an enema.
A positive target sign in a stable child is exactly the indication for enema reduction.

questions.q: A stable 14-month-old has a positive ultrasound, no peritoneal signs, and no free air on radiograph. What does the module say happens next?
ch: Discharge home with oral rehydration and a scheduled return visit in 48 hours
Broad-spectrum antibiotics alone, to shrink the hypertrophied Peyer patches
Barium enema, chosen specifically for its safety if the bowel should perforate
Immediate laparotomy with resection of the involved bowel segment
NPO status, IV access, isotonic fluids, and pneumatic (air) enema with surgery on standby
questions.exp: A stable child with a positive ultrasound and no peritonitis goes to air enema after being made NPO with IV access and isotonic fluids, with surgery on standby because of the tension pneumoperitoneum risk.
why: Intussusception is an obstruction requiring reduction, not outpatient rehydration.
Antibiotics are empiric coverage when ischemia or surgery is anticipated, not a reduction method.
Barium is generally avoided because of peritoneal soiling if perforation occurs.
Operative reduction is for failed enema, perforation, peritonitis, shock, or a lead point.

questions.q: A 5-year-old presents with his second episode of intussusception in six months. What does the module direct you to look for?
ch: Chronic constipation with stool impaction acting as the obstructing mass
A missed diagnosis, since intussusception does not recur after enema reduction
A pathologic lead point such as a Meckel diverticulum, polyp, lymphoma, or HSP hematoma
Reinfection with rotavirus from an incompletely administered vaccine series
An inherited disorder of colonic motility explaining the recurrent invagination
questions.exp: In atypical ages (under 3 months or over 2 years) and in recurrent cases the module says to hunt for a pathologic lead point, with Meckel diverticulum the classic pediatric culprit.
why: Constipation is not among the lead points or mechanisms the module lists.
Recurrence occurs in up to about 10% after enema reduction, so it is expected, not impossible.
The vaccine link concerns the withdrawn RotaShield product and a small attributable risk, not recurrence workup.
The module does not describe an inherited motility disorder as a cause.

questions.q: A 10-month-old is admitted after successful air enema reduction. Which development in the next 24 to 72 hours should prompt urgent reassessment?
ch: A single loose stool as bowel function returns and oral intake resumes
Return of colicky pain or vomiting, which may signal recurrence
Mild fussiness that settles fully when the infant is held and fed
Passage of flatus followed by tolerating a small volume of formula
A transient rise in appetite once the obstruction has been relieved
questions.exp: Recurrence follows enema reduction in up to about 10% of children and typically presents as returning colicky pain or vomiting within 24 to 72 hours, so monitoring for it is built into the disposition plan.
why: Passing stool is a sign of returning bowel function, which the module frames as reassuring.
Fussiness that settles completely does not match the episodic colicky pain of recurrence.
Passing air and tolerating oral intake are the recovery signs the nurse is watching for.
Improved feeding after relief of the obstruction is an expected part of recovery.

questions.q: During a pneumatic enema an infant abruptly develops respiratory distress with a tense, distended abdomen. What is happening and what is needed?
ch: Tension pneumoperitoneum from perforation, needing immediate needle decompression and surgery
A vasovagal response to the rectal catheter, managed by pausing and reassuring
Swallowed air from crying, managed by placing a nasogastric tube for venting
Contrast aspiration into the airway, managed with suction and supplemental oxygen
Anaphylaxis to the enema contrast, managed with intramuscular epinephrine
questions.exp: Tension pneumoperitoneum is the post-reduction catastrophe of air enema: sudden respiratory distress requiring immediate needle decompression and surgery, which is why surgery must be on standby.
why: A vasovagal episode does not produce a tense, distended abdomen with respiratory distress.
Swallowed air does not explain acute distress during insufflation under pressure.
Air, not liquid contrast, is being insufflated during a pneumatic enema.
Air enema uses no contrast agent, so a reaction to contrast is not the mechanism.

questions.q: Which triad does the module give as classic for infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?
ch: Fever, refusal to feed, and a hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis
Non-bilious projectile vomiting, a palpable olive, and hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis
Painless bloody stool, brisk weight gain, and a normal serum bicarbonate
Bilious vomiting, a distended abdomen, and a metabolic acidosis
Colicky pain, currant jelly stool, and a sausage-shaped abdominal mass
questions.exp: The classic triad is non-bilious projectile vomiting, a palpable olive in the epigastrium, and a hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis.
why: The metabolic picture is an alkalosis from lost gastric HCl, not an acidosis.
Bloody stool and weight gain are not features of gastric outlet obstruction in this module.
Bilious vomiting points away from pyloric stenosis and toward malrotation with volvulus.
Colicky pain with currant jelly stool and a sausage-shaped mass describes intussusception.

questions.q: Which laboratory pattern is the module's lab fingerprint of pyloric stenosis?
ch: Elevated lactate with an anion gap metabolic acidosis
Isolated hypoglycemia with otherwise normal electrolytes
Hyperkalemia with a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis
Hypernatremic dehydration with a respiratory alkalosis
Low chloride, low potassium, and an elevated bicarbonate
questions.exp: Persistent vomiting of gastric HCl produces a hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis - low chloride, low potassium, elevated bicarbonate - with a late paradoxical aciduria.
why: Lactic acidosis is not the described picture; loss of gastric acid raises the bicarbonate.
Hypoglycemia is a risk while NPO but is not the characteristic electrolyte fingerprint.
The potassium falls rather than rises, and the disturbance is an alkalosis.
The module describes a metabolic alkalosis from acid loss, not a respiratory one.

questions.q: Which presentation best fits the module's description of pyloric stenosis?
ch: A 4-week-old firstborn male with non-bilious vomiting who refeeds eagerly
A 3-year-old with intermittent vomiting and bloody stool after a viral illness
A 2-month-old with effortless post-feed regurgitation and normal weight gain
A 6-month-old with bilious vomiting who has no interest in feeding at all
A newborn vomiting from the first day of life with abdominal distension
questions.exp: The classic case is a 3-to-6-week-old, often a firstborn male, with progressive non-bilious vomiting who stays hungry and refeeds eagerly; the condition is not present at birth but develops over the first weeks of life.
why: Vomiting with bloody stool after a viral illness in a toddler suggests intussusception.
Effortless regurgitation with normal growth describes GERD, which lacks the olive and alkalosis.
Bilious vomiting flips the differential toward malrotation with midgut volvulus.
Pyloric stenosis is not present at birth; it develops over the first weeks of life.

questions.q: Which ultrasound measurements does the module give as diagnostic thresholds for pyloric stenosis?
ch: Antral diameter over 30 mm with free peritoneal fluid clearly present
Bowel wall thickness of 2 mm with a target sign on the transverse view
Pyloric muscle wall thickness of 3 mm or more with channel length of 14 to 16 mm or more
Gastric wall thickness under 1 mm with a pyloric channel shorter than 5 mm
Pyloric wall thickness of 10 mm or more with a channel of any measured length
questions.exp: Abdominal ultrasound is the imaging gold standard, with diagnostic thresholds of pyloric muscle wall thickness of at least 3 mm and channel length of at least 14 to 16 mm.
why: Antral diameter and free peritoneal fluid are not the criteria the module gives.
A target sign on transverse view is the ultrasound finding of intussusception.
These values fall below the diagnostic thresholds and describe a normal pylorus.
Ten millimetres far exceeds the 3 mm threshold the module actually cites.

questions.q: A 5-week-old with pyloric stenosis is dehydrated, with a chloride of 88 and a potassium of 2.9. What is the priority?
ch: Give an oral macrolide to reduce pyloric inflammation before any surgery
Book pyloromyotomy immediately, since the obstruction is a surgical emergency
Isotonic fluid resuscitation and correction of electrolytes before anesthesia
Start ondansetron to stop the vomiting, then feed the infant slowly by mouth
Place a nasogastric tube and begin continuous feeding through the pylorus
questions.exp: This is a medical resuscitation before a surgical problem: give isotonic fluids and normalize chloride, potassium, and bicarbonate before anesthesia, because operating on an alkalotic, hypokalemic infant risks postoperative apnea and arrhythmia.
why: Macrolides are a risk factor for the disease, not a treatment for it.
Pyloromyotomy is not an emergency; the metabolic derangement is what must be fixed first.
Antiemetics do not treat a mechanical obstruction and can mask progression.
The infant is kept NPO; the gastric outlet is obstructed, so enteral feeding is not the answer.

questions.q: When may potassium chloride be added to this infant's maintenance IV fluids?
ch: Only if the serum bicarbonate has already fallen below the normal range
Immediately on arrival, given as an undiluted intravenous push
Only after the pyloromyotomy has been completed in the operating room
Never, because the hypokalemia corrects on its own once vomiting stops
Only once urine output is established, with serum potassium and ECG monitoring
questions.exp: KCl is added only after urine output is established, with monitoring of serum potassium and the ECG, and undiluted IV potassium is never given by push.
why: Replacement is tied to urine output, not to waiting for the bicarbonate to fall.
Undiluted IV potassium push is explicitly forbidden in the module.
Potassium is corrected before anesthesia, not after the operation is finished.
Correcting hypokalemia is part of the preoperative plan, not something left to resolve itself.

questions.q: How does the module explain the paradoxical aciduria seen late in pyloric stenosis?
ch: Hypoglycemia forces ketone excretion, which acidifies the urine directly
Vomited hydrochloric acid is reabsorbed from the stomach and cleared renally
Renal tubular acidosis develops from the chronic vomiting and dehydration
Volume depletion drives aldosterone, which reabsorbs sodium at the expense of potassium and hydrogen
The kidney excretes the excess bicarbonate generated by the gastric mucosa
questions.exp: Volume depletion stimulates aldosterone, which reabsorbs sodium in exchange for potassium and hydrogen ions; that renal acid loss produces hypokalemia and an acid urine despite the systemic alkalosis.
why: Hypoglycemia is a separate risk of being NPO and is not the mechanism given.
Acid is lost in the emesis; it is not reabsorbed and then re-excreted.
The module attributes the finding to aldosterone-driven volume conservation, not renal tubular acidosis.
Bicarbonate is retained rather than excreted, which is why the alkalosis persists.

questions.q: A 4-week-old is referred for suspected pyloric stenosis, but the vomiting is described as green. What does the module say to do with that detail?
ch: Proceed with pyloromyotomy, because the palpable olive remains the deciding finding
Attribute it to reflux of duodenal contents through the hypertrophied pylorus
Start high-dose antiemetics and repeat the abdominal ultrasound in one week
Treat it as malrotation with midgut volvulus, a surgical emergency needing immediate evaluation
Ignore the colour, since bile staining is common once vomiting becomes forceful
questions.exp: Bilious (green) vomiting is NOT pyloric stenosis, because that obstruction is proximal to the ampulla of Vater; the differential flips to malrotation with midgut volvulus, a surgical emergency.
why: Green vomiting argues against pyloric stenosis, so operating on that assumption is unsafe.
Pyloric obstruction is proximal to the ampulla of Vater, so bile should not appear in the emesis.
Antiemetics are not indicated, and delay in suspected volvulus risks losing bowel.
The module makes bilious versus non-bilious the reflex question precisely because it changes the diagnosis.

questions.q: A caregiver panics on the first postoperative day because the infant vomited twice after feeds. What does the module have the nurse teach?
ch: An antiemetic should be started at home and continued for several weeks
Some emesis in the first 24 to 48 hours is expected and does not mean surgery failed
The pyloromyotomy has failed and a second operation will be needed shortly
Feeds should be stopped entirely and the infant kept NPO for a full week
The vomiting proves an incidental viral gastroenteritis was acquired in hospital
questions.exp: Postoperative teaching is that feeds are advanced gradually per protocol and that some emesis in the first 24 to 48 hours is expected; it does not mean the pyloromyotomy failed.
why: Antiemetics are not part of the module's plan for this condition.
Early emesis is anticipated and is not evidence of a failed pyloromyotomy.
Feeds are advanced gradually per protocol rather than withheld for a week.
The module explains the emesis as an expected postoperative finding, not a new infection.

questions.q: Which exposure does the module tell you to screen for in the history of an infant with suspected pyloric stenosis?
ch: Postnatal macrolide exposure such as erythromycin or azithromycin
Rotavirus vaccination given at the two-month well-child visit
Exclusive breastfeeding from the first day after delivery
Prenatal exposure to maternal rubella in early pregnancy
Maternal use of prenatal vitamins during the third trimester
questions.exp: Postnatal macrolide exposure - erythromycin or azithromycin, especially in the first two weeks of life - is listed alongside firstborn male sex and family history as a risk factor to screen for.
why: Rotavirus vaccine is linked to intussusception risk, not to pyloric stenosis.
Breastfeeding is not listed as a risk factor for this condition.
Maternal rubella is associated with congenital heart disease, specifically PDA.
Prenatal vitamins are not among the risk factors described.

questions.q: Which definition matches the module's description of a febrile seizure?
ch: A seizure with fever in a child 6 months to 5 years, without CNS infection or prior afebrile seizures
A seizure occurring only during the defervescence phase of a bacterial illness
A generalized convulsion that requires an abnormal EEG before it can be diagnosed
A seizure with fever in any child who also has a known epilepsy syndrome
Any convulsion in a child under 10 years, regardless of temperature or history
questions.exp: A febrile seizure is an age-limited seizure with fever (typically 38C or higher) in a child 6 months to 5 years, without CNS infection, metabolic derangement, or previous afebrile seizures.
why: The module ties the seizure to the rate and height of temperature rise, not to defervescence.
EEG is explicitly not indicated for a simple febrile seizure; the diagnosis is clinical.
A prior afebrile seizure or established epilepsy takes the case outside this definition.
The definition is bounded by the 6 month to 5 year age window and requires fever.

questions.q: Which features define a SIMPLE febrile seizure in the module's classification?
ch: Focal onset, under 5 minutes, with normal postictal mental status
Any duration, as long as the child has a documented source of fever
Two episodes in 24 hours, each of them shorter than 10 minutes
Generalized, over 15 minutes, with a prolonged postictal period
Generalized, under 15 minutes, and a single episode within 24 hours
questions.exp: Simple febrile seizures are generalized, last under 15 minutes, and occur once in 24 hours; focal features, duration over 15 minutes, or recurrence within 24 hours make the seizure complex.
why: Focal features make a febrile seizure complex, whatever its duration.
Duration matters: 15 minutes is the dividing line between simple and complex.
Recurrence within 24 hours is one of the criteria that defines a complex seizure.
A seizure over 15 minutes with a prolonged postictal state is complex, not simple.

questions.q: What does the module say about scheduled antipyretics in a child with a history of febrile seizures?
ch: They reliably prevent recurrence and should be given around the clock in fevers
They should be replaced by a daily prophylactic anticonvulsant in every case
They are used for comfort and fever reduction but do NOT prevent recurrence
They are contraindicated because lowering the temperature triggers seizures
They work only if the child's temperature is held below 36.5C at all times
questions.exp: Antipyretics are for comfort and fever reduction only; they do not prevent recurrence of febrile seizures, which the module calls a favorite exam distractor.
why: The module states directly that antipyretics do not prevent recurrence.
Daily prophylactic anticonvulsants are generally not recommended for simple febrile seizures.
Antipyretics are recommended for comfort, not contraindicated.
No such temperature target is given, and round-the-clock dosing does not prevent recurrence.

questions.q: A 2-year-old had a single 3-minute generalized convulsion with fever from an obvious viral illness and is back to baseline with a normal exam. Which workup does the module support?
ch: A basic metabolic panel, CBC, and blood culture drawn routinely
Non-contrast head CT to exclude a structural lesion as the trigger
No routine labs, EEG, or neuroimaging for a simple febrile seizure with a reassuring exam
EEG and MRI of the brain before discharge from the emergency department
Lumbar puncture for every child who has had any seizure with fever
questions.exp: Routine labs, EEG, and neuroimaging are not indicated for a simple febrile seizure with a reassuring exam; the module calls them low-yield and a source of unnecessary cost and radiation.
why: Routine labs are explicitly not indicated in this scenario.
CT adds radiation without yield in a classic simple febrile seizure.
EEG and MRI are reserved for complex features, a prolonged postictal state, or focal deficits.
LP is considered selectively - meningeal signs, under-immunized infants 6 to 12 months, or antibiotic pretreatment.

questions.q: In which situation does the module say lumbar puncture should be considered after a febrile seizure?
ch: Any child with a family history of febrile seizures in a sibling
An infant 6 to 12 months old who is under-immunized for Hib and pneumococcus
A 4-year-old with a brief generalized seizure and a clear ear infection
Any child in whom antipyretics failed to lower the temperature quickly
Every child whose temperature exceeded 39C during the febrile illness
questions.exp: LP is considered when meningeal signs are present, in infants 6 to 12 months who are under-immunized for Hib and pneumococcus, or in children pretreated with antibiotics that could mask meningitis.
why: Family history reflects genetic predisposition and does not by itself prompt an LP.
A brief generalized seizure with an identified fever source and reassuring exam does not need LP.
Response to antipyretics is not a criterion; antibiotic pretreatment is.
Height of fever alone is not one of the module's LP triggers.

questions.q: A child's febrile seizure has now continued for five minutes in the emergency department. What is first-line?
ch: Intravenous acetaminophen to bring the temperature down as fast as possible
A loading dose of levetiracetam given before any benzodiazepine is tried
Physical restraint and a bite block to protect the tongue and the teeth
Observation alone, since all febrile seizures terminate spontaneously
An intravenous benzodiazepine such as lorazepam, with airway support ready
questions.exp: A seizure lasting 5 minutes or more is febrile status epilepticus, and first-line abortive therapy is a benzodiazepine - IV lorazepam or IV/IO diazepam - with monitoring for respiratory depression and hypotension.
why: Antipyretics do not stop a seizure; they are given for comfort and fever reduction.
Levetiracetam is second-line, for benzodiazepine-refractory febrile status epilepticus.
The module says never to restrain the child or place anything in the mouth.
Most seizures self-terminate, but at 5 minutes the module calls for abortive therapy.

questions.q: Which nursing actions does the module direct during an active febrile seizure?
ch: Place the child prone with the head lower than the chest to aid drainage
Begin chest compressions as soon as the convulsion is recognized
Hold the limbs still and insert a padded airway between the teeth
Turn the child on their side, clear the area, do not restrain, and time the seizure
Sit the child upright and offer oral acetaminophen as soon as possible
questions.exp: During the event the nurse protects the airway and prevents injury: side-lying position, clear the area, no restraint and nothing in the mouth, and time the seizure while monitoring ABCs and oxygen saturation.
why: The module specifies side-lying positioning, not a prone head-down position.
Compressions are for pulselessness; a convulsing child with a pulse needs airway protection.
Restraining the child and placing objects in the mouth are both explicitly prohibited.
Nothing is given by mouth during a seizure, and antipyretics do not stop it.

questions.q: Parents of a child who has had a first simple febrile seizure ask about the future. Which numbers does the module have you give them?
ch: A 25% risk of death unless daily anticonvulsant prophylaxis is started
Roughly 30 to 35% recurrence and about a 1 to 2% risk of later epilepsy
Nearly universal recurrence and a 50% chance of developing epilepsy
About 5% recurrence and no measurable increase in epilepsy risk at all
A 10% risk of permanent brain damage from each additional seizure
questions.exp: The counseling numbers are about one in three for recurrence (30 to 35%) and only a 1 to 2% risk of epilepsy after a simple febrile seizure, with higher epilepsy risk when there are complex features, family history, or neurodevelopmental abnormality.
why: Simple febrile seizures do not cause death, and daily prophylaxis is not recommended.
These figures are far above the module's stated risks and would frighten a family needlessly.
Recurrence is about one in three, not one in twenty.
The module states that simple febrile seizures do not cause brain damage.

questions.q: Which factor does the module name as the single biggest predictor of recurrent febrile seizures?
ch: Young age at the first seizure, under about 12 to 18 months
The peak temperature recorded during the first febrile illness
Whether the seizure followed a vaccination rather than a virus
The number of days of fever before the seizure occurred
Whether antipyretics were given on a scheduled basis at home
questions.exp: Young age at the first seizure - under roughly 12 to 18 months - is named as the single biggest predictor of recurrence.
why: The module invokes the rate and height of temperature rise in pathophysiology, not peak fever as the recurrence predictor.
Post-vaccination fever is listed as a less common trigger, not as the recurrence predictor.
Duration of fever before the seizure is not the predictor the module names.
Scheduled antipyretics do not change the recurrence risk at all.

questions.q: An 8-month-old has a seizure with fever and, on exam, has a bulging fontanelle, meningismus, and a petechial rash while remaining lethargic. What does the module require?
ch: Discharge with reassurance, since a febrile seizure is a benign diagnosis
Scheduled antipyretics and a follow-up visit with the pediatrician in a week
Rectal diazepam prescribed for home use as the definitive management step
Urgent evaluation for meningitis or sepsis, with antibiotics not delayed for LP or imaging
An outpatient EEG to distinguish a febrile seizure from an epilepsy syndrome
questions.exp: Meningismus, a bulging fontanelle, a petechial rash, or persistently altered mental status are red flags for meningitis or sepsis; evaluate urgently and do not delay empiric antibiotics for LP or imaging in a toxic-appearing child.
why: A febrile seizure is a diagnosis of the well-appearing, back-to-baseline child, and this child is neither.
Antipyretics and routine follow-up do not address a suspected CNS infection.
Rescue benzodiazepines abort prolonged seizures; they do not treat meningitis.
EEG is low-yield here and would delay treatment of possible bacterial meningitis.

questions.q: Which question does the module call the pivotal one in evaluating a congenital heart defect?
ch: Whether the hemoglobin is elevated from chronic hypoxemia
Whether the lesion is cyanotic or acyanotic, and whether flow is ductal-dependent
Whether the murmur is heard best in systole or in diastole
Whether the defect formed before or after week 8 of gestation
Whether the infant was born vaginally or by cesarean delivery
questions.exp: The pivotal question is cyanotic versus acyanotic, and whether the lesion is ductal-dependent - that is, whether pulmonary or systemic flow relies on a patent ductus arteriosus.
why: Polycythemia can follow chronic hypoxemia but is not the organizing question.
Murmur timing helps localize a lesion but is not the pivotal framing question.
Cardiac development occurs in weeks 3 to 8, but that timing is not the clinical pivot.
Mode of delivery is not part of the module's classification of these defects.

questions.q: Which lesion does the module identify as the most common congenital heart defect overall?
ch: Tetralogy of Fallot
Transposition of the great arteries
Ventricular septal defect
Total anomalous pulmonary venous return
Coarctation of the aorta
questions.exp: VSD is the most common congenital heart defect overall, and small ones - which produce the louder murmur - often close spontaneously.
why: Tetralogy of Fallot is the classic cyanotic lesion but not the most common defect overall.
Transposition is a cyanotic mixing lesion linked to maternal diabetes, not the most common.
TAPVR is one of the five T's of cyanotic disease and is uncommon.
Coarctation is an acyanotic obstructive lesion, not the most common defect.

questions.q: A fixed, widely split S2 on auscultation should make you think of which defect?
ch: Ventricular septal defect
Patent ductus arteriosus
Tetralogy of Fallot
Coarctation of the aorta
Atrial septal defect
questions.exp: A fixed, widely split S2 means atrial septal defect until proven otherwise.
why: VSD produces a harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border.
PDA is an acyanotic shunt lesion classically linked to maternal rubella.
Tetralogy of Fallot gives a single S2 with a systolic murmur.
Coarctation presents with weak femoral pulses and upper-extremity hypertension.

questions.q: A cyanotic newborn is placed on 100% oxygen and the PaO2 barely rises. How does the module interpret this hyperoxia test?
ch: A cyanotic cardiac lesion is present rather than pulmonary disease
The oxygen was delivered at inadequate flow and the test should be repeated
Methemoglobinemia is the cause and methylene blue should be given
The result is normal for a newborn in the first day of life
Primary pulmonary disease such as surfactant deficiency is the likely cause
questions.exp: Failure of PaO2 to rise substantially on 100% oxygen points to a cyanotic cardiac cause rather than lung disease; cyanosis that does not improve on 100% oxygen is cyanotic congenital heart disease.
why: The flat response is itself the finding, and the module treats it as diagnostic direction.
Methemoglobinemia is not among the causes this module discusses.
A flat oxygen response is abnormal and prompts echocardiography.
Pulmonary causes of cyanosis generally do improve with supplemental oxygen.

questions.q: A neonate with a suspected ductal-dependent lesion is started on prostaglandin E1. Which complication must the team be prepared for?
ch: Malignant hyperthermia requiring dantrolene kept at the bedside
Acute closure of the ductus arteriosus within a few minutes
Severe hyperkalemia requiring calcium and insulin-dextrose
Apnea and hypotension, with intubation equipment ready at the bedside
Profound hypertension needing an intravenous beta-blocker infusion
questions.exp: PGE1 maintains ductal patency but causes apnea, hypotension, fever, and flushing, so airway and intubation equipment stay at the bedside and the infant is monitored closely.
why: Malignant hyperthermia is an anesthetic reaction; fever and flushing are the PGE1 effects described.
PGE1 keeps the duct open; indomethacin or ibuprofen is what closes it.
Hyperkalemia is a concern with ACE inhibitors, not with prostaglandin E1.
Hypotension, not hypertension, is the hemodynamic effect the module describes.

questions.q: An infant with Tetralogy of Fallot suddenly becomes deeply cyanotic and agitated, and the murmur disappears. What is the immediate nursing response?
ch: Begin chest compressions and prepare for immediate cardioversion
Start an indomethacin infusion to reduce pulmonary blood flow
Place the infant knee-chest, give oxygen, stay calm, and call the provider
Lay the infant flat and administer a rapid intravenous vasodilator
Withhold oxygen to avoid closing the ductus arteriosus prematurely
questions.exp: A hypercyanotic Tet spell - sudden deep cyanosis, agitation, and disappearance of the murmur - is managed with knee-chest positioning, oxygen, calming the infant, and calling the provider, because knee-chest raises systemic vascular resistance and reduces right-to-left shunting.
why: A Tet spell is a shunting emergency, not a pulseless arrhythmia.
Indomethacin closes a PDA and is avoided in ductal-dependent physiology.
Agents that drop systemic vascular resistance worsen the right-to-left shunt and are avoided.
Oxygen is part of treating a Tet spell, along with morphine and IV fluids.

questions.q: Which examination findings does the module tie to coarctation of the aorta?
ch: Bounding pulses in all four extremities with a continuous murmur
A fixed split S2 with a soft systolic murmur in the pulmonic area
Hepatomegaly with a gallop and a harsh holosystolic murmur
Weak or delayed femoral pulses with upper-extremity hypertension
Equal pre- and post-ductal saturations with a single loud S2
questions.exp: Weak or delayed femoral pulses with upper-extremity hypertension point to coarctation, and a right-hand versus foot gradient on pre- and post-ductal pulse oximetry suggests a ductal or coarctation lesion.
why: The hallmark is diminished lower-extremity pulses, not bounding pulses everywhere.
A fixed split S2 is the atrial septal defect finding.
Hepatomegaly with a gallop reflects decompensated heart failure, and a holosystolic murmur suggests VSD.
Coarctation produces a pre- to post-ductal saturation gradient rather than equal saturations.

questions.q: A large ventricular septal defect is left unrepaired for years and the child, previously acyanotic, becomes cyanotic. What has happened?
ch: Tetralogy of Fallot has developed on top of the septal defect over time
Eisenmenger syndrome: pulmonary vascular resistance rose until the shunt reversed
The ductus arteriosus has reopened and is now shunting from right to left
The defect has spontaneously closed, trapping blood in the right ventricle
Chronic diuretic therapy has produced a hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis
questions.exp: Eisenmenger syndrome: a chronic uncorrected left-to-right shunt raises pulmonary vascular resistance until the shunt reverses and cyanosis develops - which is a reason to repair early.
why: Tetralogy of Fallot is a congenital outflow-tract malformation, not an acquired one.
The module attributes late cyanosis here to rising pulmonary vascular resistance, not a reopened duct.
Spontaneous closure of a small VSD resolves the shunt rather than causing cyanosis.
Diuretic-induced alkalosis is an electrolyte problem and does not cause cyanosis.

questions.q: Why does the module warn against indomethacin or ibuprofen in an infant with a suspected ductal-dependent lesion?
ch: They interact with digoxin and produce fatal bradycardia in neonates
They cause apnea and hypotension identical to prostaglandin E1
They inhibit aldosterone and cause a hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis
They raise pulmonary vascular resistance and precipitate a Tet spell
They close the ductus arteriosus, the opposite of what PGE1 is doing
questions.exp: Indomethacin and ibuprofen close a hemodynamically significant PDA by inhibiting prostaglandins - the opposite effect of PGE1 - so they are avoided in ductal-dependent lesions where the duct supplies pulmonary or systemic flow.
why: The module's digoxin cautions concern its narrow therapeutic index, hypokalemia, and bradycardia.
Apnea and hypotension are the adverse effects listed for PGE1 itself.
These drugs inhibit prostaglandins; they are not aldosterone antagonists.
Their action is prostaglandin inhibition and duct closure, not a rise in pulmonary vascular resistance.

questions.q: A cyanotic newborn has a single S2, a systolic murmur, and a boot-shaped heart on chest radiograph. Which lesion and components fit?
ch: Tetralogy of Fallot: pulmonary stenosis, RVH, overriding aorta, and VSD
Atrial septal defect, with a fixed split S2 and a normal cardiac contour
Transposition of the great arteries, with an egg-on-a-string silhouette
Coarctation of the aorta, with a 3-sign and rib notching on the film
Total anomalous pulmonary venous return, with a snowman silhouette
questions.exp: A boot-shaped heart with a single S2 and systolic murmur is Tetralogy of Fallot, whose components are PROVe - pulmonary stenosis, right ventricular hypertrophy, overriding aorta, and VSD - with the degree of RVOT obstruction driving cyanosis.
why: ASD is acyanotic and gives a fixed split S2 with a different chest film.
Transposition gives the egg-on-a-string silhouette, not the boot shape.
Coarctation is acyanotic and shows the 3-sign with rib notching.
TAPVR produces the snowman or figure-8 silhouette.
